title: Jenny Wiley’s captivity and escape
summary: Taken captive in a 1789 raid on her Virginia cabin, Jenny Wiley spent nearly eleven months held in the Big Sandy country before she managed to escape.
bodyMarkdown:
On October 1, 1789, a war party struck a cabin on Walker's Creek in what is now Bland County, Virginia. The raiders, usually described as Cherokee and Shawnee men, were looking for revenge on Matthias Harman, a frontiersman they blamed for earlier killings. Instead they found the home of his neighbor, Thomas Wiley, who was away.

[Jenny Wiley](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jenny_Wiley), born Virginia Sellards, was home with her children and her younger brother. Her brother and three of her children were killed in the attack. Jenny, pregnant, was taken captive with her infant son, and the party set off west toward the Big Sandy country of what would become eastern Kentucky.

The infant could not keep up and was killed on the trail. Jenny was held for nearly eleven months, moved from camp to camp in the hills and hollows. A child born to her in captivity was also killed. Accounts of the captivity come mostly from family tradition written down long afterward, so the details vary from telling to telling.

Her escape is the best-known part of the story. In the summer of 1790, while her captors were away, she slipped out of camp. Family tradition says she followed creeks she had seen in a dream until she reached the Big Sandy's Levisa Fork, across from Harman's Station, a new blockhouse near present Paintsville. Men at the station built a rough log raft and pulled her across just as her pursuers reached the far bank.

From there she made her way home to Virginia and to Thomas. The couple later had more children. Around 1800 they moved back to the land where she had been held, settling on Tom's Creek in what became Johnson County. Thomas died in 1810. Jenny Wiley lived there until her death in 1831 and is buried near the creek.

## Kentucky today

Jenny Wiley State Resort Park, on Dewey Lake near Prestonsburg in Floyd County, carries her name. A long-distance hiking route, the Jenny Wiley Heritage Trail, traces parts of her path, and her grave is in Johnson County.
